questions: What two numbers did we divide to get the 5 metres per second?
What single extra fact turns that speed into a velocity?
segments.say: Velocity is speed with a direction. Watch the athlete sprint the track from 0 to 100 metres in 20 seconds, then do the division with me: 100 over 20 is 5 metres per second. Keep your student notes open at the speed and velocity definitions for this scene.

questions: Why does the gradient of this graph carry speed units?
What would a steeper line in the same axes mean?
segments.say: Distance-time graphs: the gradient is the speed. Ride the probe up the line as it climbs 120 metres in 60 seconds, and watch the gradient triangle build underneath - rise over run, 120 over 60, is 2 metres per second. Now try the gradient question on the worksheet in pairs.

questions: Which graph reading gives acceleration, and which gives distance?
How would the shaded area change if the line rose twice as fast?
segments.say: Velocity-time graphs: slope is acceleration, area is distance. The line rises from 0 to 20 metres per second in 10 seconds, so the slope is 2 metres per second squared - and watch the shaded area grow under the line: that area is the 100 metres travelled. Check the area rule in your student notes.

questions: Why do the outward and return legs cancel for velocity but not for speed?
What would the average velocity be if the runner stopped at the far end instead?
segments.say: Check the thinking. The runner jogs 400 metres down the track and back in 100 seconds: distance 800 metres, speed 8 metres per second - but displacement zero, so velocity zero. Then take the exit ticket on your own - its first question revisits the flat-line claim head-on.
segments.watchFor: A flat line on a velocity-time graph means the object has stopped. Listen for it in pair talk and watch for it on the exit ticket: Flat reads as "nothing is happening", so the line feels like zero movement. Send them back to the flat line at a steady height and the correct turn: A flat v-t line means constant velocity: the object keeps moving at the same speed.
